doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

title: Meeting Schoenberg and the Stoloff circle in Hollywood
summary: Through Morris Stoloff's house he met Ernst Toch and Schoenberg, who told of arranging for Radio Berlin.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: You’ve had some amazing friends and associates over the years, including I read that you studied with Schoenberg?

Schoenberg — after the war Arnold Schoenberg was in Hollywood. He was somewhat of a refugee, not politically but musically. You know he was lost in Germany and Austria. It was a bad time to go back. And he had friends. There was a man by the name of Morris Stoloff who was music director at Columbia Pictures. And he announced that he and his wife were kind of the home in Hollywood of Stravinsky, Mr. Rachmaninoff, Horowitz, who was on his sabbatical — he was practicing but not playing for the public, and Ernst Toch and Schoenberg, people like that, the Stoloff house was a gathering place. And for some reason I played piano on a date for Morris, something that Ernst Toch had written that was incredibly difficult technically according to the house pianist, and I of course waltzed through it because I had no brains just courage. So I became a member of a very kind of funny, a lonesome, elite society. And then when Mr. Schoenberg started teaching

at UCLA he was very unhappy because most of the kids slept, they just went there for a credit of some kind, you know they’d nod through class. And I had the audacity once to say, I was then working in Metro, that I’d like really to take a score and show it to him. And that opened a dam because he then told me that he was a radio arranger in Radio Berlin at the same time that Dmitri Shostakovich was a radio arranger in Moscow, and that the arrangement of “Tea for Two” which has become famous, of Shostakovich, Mr. Schoenberg said, “I did fifty of those, none of them ever became famous.” He was a strange, strange man. I was frightened to death of him. He wore — like I’m dressed today — in California he wore black and he didn’t like sunlight. So strange to be a refugee in California.
